derivation_notes: Under diploid Wright-Fisher sampling, the next-generation focal-allele count X is distributed as Binomial(2*N, p), so p_next = X/(2*N). Since delta_p = p_next - p and p is fixed across replicates conditional on the inputs, Var(delta_p) = Var(X)/(2*N)**2 = p*(1 - p)/(2*N).

The target is a sampling statistic rather than any single stochastic realization.

new_symbol_range_suggestions.D: D >= 0; D = 0 for ideal equal-contribution sampling, larger D for stronger reproductive skew or crowding-driven variance inflation

derivation_notes: Relax the Wright-Fisher assumption of equal realized parental contribution by introducing a reproductive-dispersion condition D that inflates the variance effective sampling term. This keeps the heterozygosity factor p*(1-p) and diploid 1/(2*N) scaling but multiplies them by an environment-dependent inflation factor that is exactly neutral when D = 0.
change_summary: A new controllable condition D promotes reproductive-dispersion context from fixed to varying across populations. The successor predicts larger drift variance at the same p and N when family-size variance or parental-contribution inequality is stronger.

assumption_audit.released_assumption: Breeders contribute independently and with equal expected reproductive success, so the finite-sampling variance is fully determined by p and N alone.
assumption_audit.mechanism: Variance effective population size is reduced when offspring number is overdispersed or parental contributions are unequal, increasing one-generation drift variance above the Wright-Fisher expectation.
assumption_audit.parent_reduction: Setting D = 0 removes the variance-inflation factor and recovers the parent law exactly.

response_change.parent_relation: With only p and N, the variance is V_delta_p = p*(1-p)/(2*N), so for any fixed N the p-dependence is a single symmetric parabola and changing population context can only be mimicked by changing the overall 1/N scale.
response_change.child_relation: Introduce a varying reproductive-dispersion condition so the effective sampling variance depends jointly on p, N, and a crowding/variance input; the p*(1-p) term is retained but its amplitude changes with the additional condition, creating a p-by-environment interaction in the target mapping.
response_change.observable_effect: At the same p and N, replicate allele-frequency variance is larger in populations with stronger reproductive skew/crowding than under ideal Wright-Fisher sampling; across that condition, the parent cannot respond at all because it ignores the varying context.

evolution_contract.activation_condition: Observable when the experiment includes populations that differ in offspring-number dispersion or unequal parental contribution while p and N are both supplied over non-boundary ranges 0<p<1 and finite N; the effect is strongest for intermediate p and smaller N.
evolution_contract.train_hidden_contrast: Training can show the baseline p and N dependence under near-ideal sampling and also some elevated-variance cases; holdout extends the same dispersion-driven inflation over new p,N combinations without changing sign, symmetry, or boundary behavior.
evolution_contract.continuation_path: In the limit of equal expected and realized reproductive contributions across breeders, the refinement collapses back to V_delta_p = p*(1-p)/(2*N).
evolution_contract.promotion_reason: The omitted mechanism is variation across populations in reproductive-dispersion conditions. Existing inputs p and N cannot distinguish ideal equal-contribution sampling from overdispersed family-size sampling at the same p and N, so one additional independently sampled static input is needed.
evolution_contract.domain_mechanism: reproductive-dispersion inflation of neutral drift variance
evolution_contract.scientific_mechanism: Variance effective population size is reduced when offspring number is overdispersed or parental contributions are unequal, increasing one-generation drift variance above the Wright-Fisher expectation.
evolution_contract.difficulty_rationale: This is harder than coefficient retuning because the scored target now depends on an additional supplied condition D, so populations with identical p and N but different reproductive dispersion must map to different V_delta_p values. A parent law with one shared parameterization and no D input is structurally unable to separate those cases.
evolution_contract.assumption_before: Breeders contribute independently and with equal expected reproductive success, so the finite-sampling variance is fully determined by p and N alone.
evolution_contract.assumption_after: Reproductive-dispersion conditions vary across populations and multiplicatively inflate the one-generation sampling variance above the Wright-Fisher baseline.
evolution_contract.observable_signature: Holding p and N fixed while varying D changes the height of the same symmetric p*(1-p) profile: D = 0 gives the parent baseline, and D > 0 yields uniformly larger variance with the same zeros at p = 0 and p = 1 and the same peak location at p = 1/2. This is observable only when the supplied dataset includes differing reproductive-dispersion conditions at shared or overlapping p,N values.
evolution_contract.shortcut_blocked: A single parent parameter set cannot reproduce the contrast because the parent has no D input channel and therefore must assign the same V_delta_p to all samples sharing p and N, regardless of reproductive skew. Refitting existing parameters globally can only change the common baseline scale, not produce distinct outputs across different D values at identical p and N.

new_symbol_range_suggestions.C: C >= 0; C = 0 recovers frequency-independent dispersion inflation, larger C gives stronger mid-frequency amplification of the D effect

derivation_notes: The parent assumes overdispersion multiplies the Wright-Fisher variance by one frequency-independent factor. Relaxing that assumption, clustered family contribution is represented by letting the dispersion multiplier increase with the symmetric mid-frequency occupancy measure 4*p*(1 - p), so excess variance from D is strongest when both alleles are broadly represented among contributing lineages.
change_summary: Added one new controllable condition C so reproductive skew no longer acts as a uniform gain across allele frequencies. The successor predicts stronger relative variance inflation near p = 0.5 and weaker inflation near p = 0 or 1 at the same N and D.

assumption_audit.released_assumption: Reproductive overdispersion inflates drift variance by the same proportional factor at all allele frequencies.
assumption_audit.mechanism: Family clustering or local crowding can make offspring-number variance couple more strongly to allele-count variance when both allelic classes are common enough to be represented across many contributing families.
assumption_audit.parent_reduction: Setting C = 0 removes the frequency-selective amplification and exactly recovers the parent expression.

response_change.parent_relation: The parent maps inputs as V_delta_p = p*(1-p)*(1+D)/(2*N), so D acts as one shared multiplicative gain independent of allele frequency shape; for fixed N, changing D rescales the same symmetric parabola in p without changing where variance inflation is strongest across p.
response_change.child_relation: Refine the overdispersion factor so reproductive skew interacts with allele frequency, making variance inflation stronger at intermediate p than near the boundaries; the p-dependence is no longer a simple shared gain on p*(1-p).
response_change.observable_effect: At fixed N, two populations with the same D but different starting p values show different relative inflation above Wright-Fisher variance; compared with the parent's constant ratio 1+D, the child predicts a larger inflation factor near p≈0.5 and weaker inflation as p approaches 0 or 1.

evolution_contract.activation_condition: Observable when reproductive dispersion is nonzero (D>0) and allele frequencies span interior values, especially comparing mid-frequency p≈0.5 against near-boundary p<<0.5 or 1-p<<0.5, while holding N fixed.
evolution_contract.train_hidden_contrast: Within training, variation over p and D already reveals whether dispersion acts as a uniform multiplier or is amplified at intermediate frequencies; in holdout, the same mechanism extends to stronger D or more extreme p where the divergence in relative inflation becomes clearer.
evolution_contract.continuation_path: Recover the parent law in the limit where reproductive-dispersion effects are frequency-independent, e.g. when the added interaction strength tends to zero or under idealized equal-contribution sampling D=0.
evolution_contract.promotion_reason: A frequency-dependent sensitivity of drift inflation to reproductive skew requires one extra independently varied condition describing how assortative family clustering or local crowding couples offspring-number variance to allele-frequency composition; existing p, N, and D alone only encode mean frequency, census size, and overall dispersion magnitude, which cannot distinguish uniform from frequency-selective variance inflation.
evolution_contract.domain_mechanism: frequency-dependent amplification of reproductive-skew variance by family clustering
evolution_contract.scientific_mechanism: In realistic skewed reproduction with family clustering or local patch contributions, the effect of offspring-number variance on sampled allele counts can depend on how both alleles are distributed among contributing families, producing stronger excess variance when both alleles are common enough to be represented across competing family lineages.
evolution_contract.difficulty_rationale: This is harder than a coefficient-only correction because the new input C enters inside the dispersion multiplier through the combined quantity 4*p*(1 - p), creating a nested p-by-D interaction that changes the relative inflation profile across p rather than merely rescaling all observations.
evolution_contract.assumption_before: Breeders contribute independently and with equal expected reproductive success is already relaxed only through a single frequency-independent dispersion multiplier D.
evolution_contract.assumption_after: A separate clustering condition C modulates how strongly reproductive dispersion is amplified at intermediate allele frequencies through the symmetric occupancy factor 4*p*(1 - p).
evolution_contract.parent_reduction: Set C = 0 to recover p*(1 - p)*(1 + D)/(2*N).
evolution_contract.observable_signature: Holding N fixed and comparing the same nonzero D across p, the parent predicts a constant relative inflation V_delta_p / (p*(1 - p)/(2*N)) = 1 + D, whereas the child predicts 1 + D*(1 + C*4*p*(1 - p)), which peaks at p = 0.5 and declines toward 1 + D near p = 0 or 1. This changes the scored target mapping itself, not merely an auxiliary trajectory.
evolution_contract.shortcut_blocked: A single refit of the parent parameters cannot reproduce both the mid-frequency enhancement and the near-boundary weakening at common D, because the parent enforces one p-independent inflation ratio for all allele frequencies. Adjusting D or N only changes a shared gain and cannot generate the p-dependent contrast observed when C>0.

evolution_plan.rationale: The parent response is a fixed parabola in p whose height is scaled uniformly by 1+D, so for any fixed N the ratio V_delta_p/[p*(1-p)/(2*N)] is constant across p. The effect must still preserve nonnegativity, allele-label symmetry, and vanishing variance at p=0 and p=1. Limitation: this refinement needs one new experimental condition describing the family-structure or clustering regime, because with only p, N, and D observed, any frequency dependence cannot be identified separately from the overall gain.

derivation_notes: The parent already modulates reproductive-dispersion inflation by the normalized heterozygosity coordinate 4*p*(1 - p); here that modulation is re-derived under diminishing returns, replacing linear growth of the clustering amplification by a saturating response in the same declared quantity. For small C*4*p*(1 - p), the new term is approximately linear and recovers the parent to first order, while for central allele frequencies it bends over because further mixing no longer increases between-family contrast proportionally.
change_summary: Changed the assumption that family-clustering amplification grows linearly across all allele mixtures, replacing it with a saturating dependence on 4*p*(1 - p). This creates observable concave flattening of variance inflation near p=1/2 at fixed N, D, and C>0.

assumption_audit.released_assumption: The family-clustering modulation of reproductive-dispersion effects grows linearly and without saturation with the intermediate-frequency coordinate 4*p*(1 - p).
assumption_audit.mechanism: Under clustered family contributions, excess drift from offspring-number skew can saturate once both alleles are already broadly represented across many contributing lineages, so additional heterozygosity yields diminishing extra between-family contrast.
assumption_audit.parent_reduction: In the weak-clustering limit C*4*p*(1 - p) << 1, the factor (C*4*p*(1 - p))/(1 + C*4*p*(1 - p)) approximates C*4*p*(1 - p), recovering the parent law to leading order.

response_change.parent_relation: At fixed N and D, excess variance from reproductive dispersion is a single monotone quadratic function of heterozygosity p*(1-p): the inflation factor is 1 + D*(1 + 4*C*p*(1-p)), so the D effect grows linearly with p*(1-p) and is maximal at p=1/2.
response_change.child_relation: Retain heterozygosity-driven inflation but relax the assumption that family-clustering amplification rises linearly across all allele mixtures; instead, allow saturation at high p*(1-p), so the D effect increases with intermediate-frequency mixing at low to moderate heterozygosity but bends over near p=1/2.
response_change.observable_effect: When N and D are held fixed and p is varied from rare-allele regimes toward p=1/2, the child predicts weaker-than-linear additional variance gain near p=1/2 compared with the parent, while remaining similar near the boundaries where p*(1-p) is small.

evolution_contract.activation_condition: Observable when D>0 and C>0, with p away from 0 and 1 so that 4*p*(1-p) is appreciable; the contrast is strongest for moderate-to-large C and p near 1/2, while it vanishes as D->0, C->0, or p approaches the allele-frequency boundaries.
evolution_contract.train_hidden_contrast: In training, the mechanism appears as stronger curvature of V_delta_p versus p under positive D and C than the parent's single linear-in-heterozygosity inflation permits; in holdout, the same mechanism extends to larger C or more central p where saturation of the clustering effect becomes more evident.
evolution_contract.continuation_path: Recover the parent law in the weak-clustering limit where the saturation correction becomes negligible, equivalently when the added nonlinearity is taken to zero so the amplification reduces back to a linear function of 4*p*(1-p).
evolution_contract.domain_mechanism: saturating family-clustering amplification of reproductive-dispersion variance inflation
evolution_contract.scientific_mechanism: Under clustered family contributions, excess drift from offspring-number skew can saturate when both alleles are already well represented across many contributing lineages, because additional heterozygosity no longer keeps increasing between-family contrast proportionally.
evolution_contract.difficulty_rationale: This embedding is structurally harder than a coefficient-only correction because the coefficient multiplying the existing clustering process now depends nonlinearly on the declared mixture coordinate 4*p*(1 - p), changing the shape of the p-to-target mapping rather than merely rescaling its amplitude.
evolution_contract.assumption_before: The parent fixes a single-phase, unsaturating dependence of dispersion inflation on intermediate-frequency allele mixing through the term 1 + 4*C*p*(1-p).
evolution_contract.assumption_after: The clustering-mediated amplification of reproductive dispersion is still driven by intermediate-frequency mixing, but it saturates at high 4*p*(1-p) instead of remaining linear across the full range.
evolution_contract.parent_reduction: In the weak-clustering limit C*4*p*(1 - p) << 1, (C*4*p*(1 - p))/(1 + C*4*p*(1 - p)) = C*4*p*(1 - p) + higher-order terms, so the child reduces to the parent law to leading order.
evolution_contract.observable_signature: Vary p while holding N, D, and C fixed with D>0 and C>0. The parent predicts an affine dependence of the dispersion-inflation factor on midmix = 4*p*(1-p), whereas the child predicts the same low-midmix onset but a concave, saturating bend near midmix close to 1; thus central allele frequencies show less extra variance than a single shared linear-in-midmix parent fit would require.
evolution_contract.shortcut_blocked: A single parent parameter set cannot reproduce this contrast because its dependence on midmix is restricted to one affine form inside the D inflation factor. Retuning D or C only changes intercept and slope uniformly across p, so it cannot match both the near-boundary behavior and the flattened central behavior across the same fixed-N, fixed-D, fixed-C conditions.

evolution_plan.activation_condition: Observable when D>0 and C>0, with p away from 0 and 1 so that 4*p*(1-p) is appreciable; the contrast is strongest for moderate-to-large C and p near 1/2, while it vanishes as D->0, C->0, or p approaches the allele-frequency boundaries.
evolution_plan.train_hidden_contrast: In training, the mechanism appears as stronger curvature of V_delta_p versus p under positive D and C than the parent's single linear-in-heterozygosity inflation permits; in holdout, the same mechanism extends to larger C or more central p where saturation of the clustering effect becomes more evident.
evolution_plan.continuation_path: Recover the parent law in the weak-clustering limit where the saturation correction becomes negligible, equivalently when the added nonlinearity is taken to zero so the amplification reduces back to a linear function of 4*p*(1-p).
evolution_plan.gap_statement: The current model assumes that the family-clustering modulation of reproductive-dispersion effects grows linearly with heterozygosity across the full admissible allele-frequency range, with no possibility of diminishing returns once both alleles are already widely represented among contributing families.
evolution_plan.baseline_assumption: The parent fixes a single-phase, unsaturating dependence of dispersion inflation on intermediate-frequency allele mixing through the term 1 + 4*C*p*(1-p).
evolution_plan.scientific_mechanism: Under clustered family contributions, excess drift from offspring-number skew can saturate when both alleles are already well represented across many contributing lineages, because additional heterozygosity no longer keeps increasing between-family contrast proportionally.
evolution_plan.rationale: A realistic next refinement is to relax the parent's linear heterozygosity amplification of the D effect, not to add a wholly new process. The parent already includes reproductive dispersion and family clustering, but it encodes them with a single-phase response: at fixed N and D, increasing p from rare values to p=1/2 always boosts the dispersion inflation at a constant rate in the coordinate 4*p*(1-p). Scientifically, if clustered reproduction causes excess variance through allele representation across families, that amplification should often show diminishing returns once both alleles are already broadly distributed among contributing families. The concrete distinguishing condition is: vary p across replicate starting frequencies while holding N, D, and C fixed with D>0 and C>0. Then the parent predicts a strictly linear increase of the inflation factor with 4*p*(1-p), whereas the child predicts concave bending or saturation near p=1/2. A single refit of the existing parent parameters cannot reproduce both the near-boundary behavior and the flattened central behavior across these p conditions, because its dependence on 4*p*(1-p) is constrained to one affine form. This changes the scored target mapping itself, not merely an auxiliary trajectory. The effect is admissible and observable only when there is nonzero dispersion inflation to modulate; if D=0, C=0, or p is near 0 or 1, the parent and child become effectively indistinguishable.

selected_embedding_pattern.description: Make the coefficient of an existing process depend on a declared quantity.

scenario_text: In a neutral diploid population, the next generation is formed by randomly sampling a finite number of parental gene copies. Across independently chosen starting allele frequencies and breeding population sizes, quantify the expected variance of the one-generation allele-frequency change among replicate populations. The target is a sampling statistic rather than any single stochastic realization.

response_change.parent_relation: At fixed N and D, excess variance from reproductive dispersion is a single monotone quadratic function of heterozygosity p*(1-p): the inflation factor is 1 + D*(1 + 4*C*p*(1-p)), so the D effect grows linearly with p*(1-p) and is maximal at p=1/2.
response_change.child_relation: Retain heterozygosity-driven inflation but relax the assumption that family-clustering amplification rises linearly across all allele mixtures; instead, allow saturation at high p*(1-p), so the D effect increases with intermediate-frequency mixing at low to moderate heterozygosity but bends over near p=1/2.
response_change.observable_effect: When N and D are held fixed and p is varied from rare-allele regimes toward p=1/2, the child predicts weaker-than-linear additional variance gain near p=1/2 compared with the parent, while remaining similar near the boundaries where p*(1-p) is small.

derivation_notes: The parent assumes a Michaelis-like dependence of clustering amplification on heterozygosity h=4*p*(1-p). Relaxing that to a steeper onset in h, by applying the saturating map to h**2 instead of h, represents sharper activation of between-family contrast only once both alleles are well represented across contributing lineages.
change_summary: The heterozygosity-dependent clustering factor was refined from a simple saturation in 4*p*(1-p) to a sharper nested saturation in (4*p*(1-p))**2. This preserves symmetry, boundary zeros, and 1/(2*N) scaling while producing a stronger center-versus-shoulder contrast in variance inflation.

assumption_audit.released_assumption: The clustering effect of reproductive overdispersion on variance inflation follows a fixed Michaelis-like saturation in the symmetric heterozygosity coordinate 4*p*(1-p).
assumption_audit.mechanism: In finite sets of contributing families or demes, between-family allele contrast can rise more abruptly once both alleles are represented across enough lineages, giving a steeper mid-frequency amplification of overdispersed sampling than a single simple saturation curve.
assumption_audit.parent_reduction: The child is a law refinement with no promoted variable; it recovers the parent only by returning the heterozygosity-modulation law to the original Michaelis form.

response_change.parent_relation: At fixed D and C, V_delta_p scales as p*(1-p) times a saturating increasing function of heterozygosity 4*p*(1-p), so the excess-variance multiplier is always concave-up-then-saturating with a single fixed saturation shape.
response_change.child_relation: Retain the same boundary zeros and N^{-1} scaling, but relax the specific Michaelis-like saturation assumption for how family-clustering modifies overdispersion, allowing a sharper mid-frequency concentration of excess variance than the parent can produce with one shared C.
response_change.observable_effect: When N and D are held fixed and p varies, the child can produce a narrower, more sharply peaked inflation around intermediate p while matching weaker inflation at moderately off-center frequencies; the parent with one shared C cannot simultaneously fit both the shoulder and the center because its heterozygosity response has one fixed saturation curvature.

evolution_contract.continuation_path: Recover the parent by returning to the specific current saturation law for heterozygosity-dependent excess variance, i.e. the sharper family-contrast refinement tends continuously back to the present Michaelis-type form in the appropriate shape limit.

evolution_contract.scientific_mechanism: In finite sets of contributing families or demes, between-family allele contrast can rise more abruptly once both alleles are represented across enough lineages, giving a steeper mid-frequency amplification of overdispersed sampling than a single simple saturation curve.
evolution_contract.difficulty_rationale: The refinement is not a coefficient rescaling: it first combines allele frequency into the heterozygosity coordinate 4*p*(1-p), then applies an additional nonlinear sharpening before the saturating map. This changes curvature of the scored p-to-variance relation in a way that a single shared parent C cannot emulate over center and shoulder frequencies simultaneously.
evolution_contract.assumption_before: The clustering effect of reproductive overdispersion on variance inflation follows a fixed Michaelis-like saturation in the symmetric heterozygosity coordinate 4*p*(1-p).
evolution_contract.assumption_after: The same clustering mechanism activates more abruptly with heterozygosity, so the saturation acts on a sharpened heterozygosity contrast rather than directly on 4*p*(1-p).
evolution_contract.parent_reduction: Return the heterozygosity-modulation law from saturation in (4*p*(1-p))**2 to saturation in 4*p*(1-p).
evolution_contract.observable_signature: At fixed N, D, and C, both parent and child remain symmetric in p and vanish at p=0 and p=1, but the child shows weaker excess variance on intermediate shoulders and a relatively sharper rise toward the peak near p=0.5. This center-versus-shoulder contrast is observable whenever interior p values sample both below and near the clustering-activation scale.
evolution_contract.shortcut_blocked: A single parent parameter set only changes the overall strength D and one fixed Michaelis curvature through C, so it cannot independently sharpen the mid-frequency peak while preserving weaker shoulder inflation across the same p sweep. Refitting D rescales all interior p similarly, and refitting C shifts one saturation scale but does not create the child's stronger suppression at moderate heterozygosity together with retained central amplification.

derivation_notes: The parent assumed that the family-clustering effect enters through a single rational saturation in the squared heterozygosity coordinate. Relaxing that assumption to a steeper lineage-mixing onset gives a higher-order heterozygosity occupancy term, so excess variance remains weaker at low heterozygosity and rises more sharply only near intermediate allele frequencies before saturating.
change_summary: Changed the heterozygosity-dependent amplification from a single-phase saturation in (4*p*(1-p))**2 to a steeper nested saturation in (4*p*(1-p))**4. This refines the drift-inflation law under clustered family contribution without adding new inputs or states.

assumption_audit.released_assumption: The frequency dependence of overdispersion effects is fully described by a single rational saturation in (4*p*(1-p))**2 with one shared curvature scale C.
assumption_audit.mechanism: A finite number of contributing family lineages or patches can make between-family allele-contrast effects emerge only after broader two-allele representation across lineages, producing a more threshold-like but still saturating dependence on heterozygosity.
assumption_audit.parent_reduction: The successor is a law refinement within the same observed-variable set; no promoted condition or state is used.

response_change.parent_relation: At fixed N and D, excess variance above p(1-p)/(2N) is a single symmetric saturating function of heterozygosity 4*p*(1-p), rising smoothly from the boundaries to one broad mid-frequency plateau controlled by one concentration scale C.
response_change.child_relation: Keep the same variables but replace the single-scale mid-frequency amplification assumption by a steeper onset around intermediate heterozygosity and a flatter shoulder near p≈1/2, so the D effect depends on heterozygosity with an additional shape change not reducible to one saturating phase.
response_change.observable_effect: When N and D are held fixed and p is varied, the child predicts weaker excess variance at low-to-moderate heterozygosity but a sharper rise into the central-frequency region, followed by similar saturation near p=1/2; one shared parent shape cannot match both the delayed onset and the steep central rise across the full p range.
